newsitem.title: DENMARK: Clinton does not rule out extended US Bosnia role.
newsitem.headline: Clinton does not rule out extended US Bosnia role.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday refused to rule out continued U.S. military involvement in Bosnia after June 30, 1998, despite Senate pressure to withdraw by then.
"I believe the present operation will have run its course by then and then we will have to discuss what, if any, involvement the U.S. should have," he told reporters during a visit to Denmark.

The House of Representatives last month voted to cut off funding for U.S. troops serving in a Bosnia stabilisation force (SFOR) next June and the Senate on Friday strongly urged, but did not require, a pullout by then.

"I will say this, our work there with the SFOR...we have fewer troops there now than when we started, it's been much less expensive and much less hazardous to America than a resumption of full-scale war would be," Clinton said.
"I think its been a very good thing we've done and I hope the American people would be very proud of it," he added.
Friday's Senate amendment, offered by Michigan Democratic Sen. Carl Levin, softened an earlier attempt by Sen. Russell Feingold, a Wisconsin Democrat, for a firmer cutoff date.
Feingold ended up backing the Levin amendment.

Russia on Friday joined Bosnian Serb leaders in condemning a NATO operation against war crimes suspects but Western envoys said the raid brought Bosnia closer to reconciliation and a more stable peace.
Clinton on Friday said the drive by NATO to arrest accused Bosnia war criminals was part of an overall attempt to salvage the Dayton peace accords.
"We basically believe that we have to make an effort to save the Dayton process," Clinton told reporters on Air Force One on his way to Denmark from Romania.
The Russian foreign ministry said the action by British special forces went beyond the NATO peacekeeping mandate and hinted Moscow might withdraw its soldiers from the operation.
Bosnian Serb leaders said the raid was an "irrational action" but stopped short of issuing threats against the 31,000-strong NATO-led force enforcing the peace accords.
The force said there were no reprisals against its troops after British special forces detained one suspect and shot dead another who opened fire when soldiers tried to arrest him.
The NATO swoop coincided with a power struggle in Serb territory between hardliners loyal to Radovan Karadzic and Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.

Clinton arrived in Copenhagen on Friday and is due to leave for Washington at around 1530 GMT on Saturday after holding talks with Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen and delivering a public speech in the city centre.
